Apple___Apple_scab.description: A fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis that primarily affects apple leaves and fruit, causing severe defoliation and blemished crops.
symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown circular velvety spots on upper leaf surfaces
Leaves become distorted, puckered, and turn yellow before premature drop
Scabby, cracked lesions on developing apple fruit
Dark olive lesions on young twigs in severe cases
management: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to eliminate overwintering fungal spores
Prune apple tree canopies annually to improve sunlight penetration and air circulation
Plant scab-resistant cultivars such as Liberty, Enterprise, or Freedom
Apply protective preventive bio-fungicides during early spring bud break before rainfall

Apple___Black_rot.description: A serious fungal disease caused by Diplodia seriata (Botryosphaeria obtusa) causing leaf frogeye spots, cankers on limbs, and firm black rot on fruit.
symptoms: Circular purple leaf specks expanding into tan centers with dark margins ('frogeye' spots)
Depressed, dark reddish-brown cankers on branches and tree bark
Fruit develops firm brown rot with alternating light and dark concentric rings
Infected fruit shrivels into black mummies that hang on branches
management: Prune out dead wood, fire blight strikes, and cankers at least 15 cm below visible lesions
Remove and bury all mummified apples remaining on trees or on the orchard floor
Avoid bark damage during mechanical cultivation and harvesting
Apply recommended copper or sulfur sprays early in the growing season

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: A heteroecious fungal disease caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae that requires both apple trees and Eastern red cedar (juniper) to complete its lifecycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange circular spots on upper leaf surfaces in early summer
Small raised black dots (pycnia) developing in the center of yellow spots
Tube-like fungal structures (aecia) producing orange-brown spores on leaf undersides
Premature leaf drop leading to weakened tree vigor and reduced fruit size
management: Remove nearby red cedar or ornamental juniper trees within 1 to 2 km of apple orchards
Prune out and destroy cedar-gall growths from nearby ornamental junipers in late winter
Grow rust-resistant apple varieties such as Redfree, Freedom, or Williams Pride
Apply preventive fungicide sprays when orange gelatinous galls appear on nearby cedars

Apple___healthy.description: The apple foliage displays optimal health with no visible symptoms of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease.
symptoms: Foliage shows vibrant, uniform green color without lesions or discoloration
Leaves are firm, well-expanded, and structurally intact
Canopy exhibits steady vegetative vigor and balanced shoot growth
Bark and twigs are smooth and free of cankers, galls, or exudates
management: Maintain consistent drip irrigation avoiding prolonged foliage wetness
Conduct regular soil tests and provide balanced nitrogen, potassium, and micronutrients
Perform balanced winter pruning to ensure optimal airflow and sun exposure
Regularly scout the orchard for early pest incursions or nutrient deficiencies

Blueberry___healthy.description: The blueberry plant displays vigorous vegetative growth and healthy dark-green leaves free of rust, leaf spots, or blight.
symptoms: Leaves display deep green color with smooth, unblemished margins
Stems are sturdy with vibrant cane color and healthy terminal buds
Root zone shows active mycorrhizal growth with healthy fine rootlets
No chlorosis, necrosis, or premature defoliation observed
management: Maintain acidic soil pH between 4.5 and 5.2 using elemental sulfur or peat moss
Mulch with pine bark or pine needles to retain root moisture and suppress weeds
Ensure uniform moisture supply, especially during flower bud set and fruit swell
Prune out older canes (over 6 years old) during late winter to encourage new shoots

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: A common fungal disease caused by Podosphaera clandestina affecting leaves and young shoots of sweet and sour cherries.
symptoms: White, powdery circular patches of fungal mycelium on lower leaf surfaces
Leaves curl upward along margins, become blistered, and develop chlorosis
Infected new shoots become stunted, distorted, and covered in white growth
Premature leaf drop leading to reduced cold-hardiness and delayed fruit ripening
management: Prune dense canopies to promote rapid drying of foliage after dew or rains
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization that stimulates overly susceptible succulent growth
Use potassium bicarbonate, horticultural mineral oils, or sulfur sprays at first sign
Collect and compost or bury fallen infected leaves during post-harvest cleanup

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: The cherry foliage exhibits excellent physiological condition with glossy, intact leaves and healthy spur development.
symptoms: Leaves are glossy, rich green, and completely free of powdery coatings or shot-holes
Fruiting spurs show strong, compact growth and healthy bud clusters
Branch terminals show balanced extension growth without wilting or flagging
Trunk and major scaffold limbs show smooth bark without bacterial gummosis
management: Provide deep, well-drained soil with adequate calcium and boron supplementation
Apply reflective orchard mulch or organic matter to cool soil temperatures
Perform summer pruning to manage tree height and improve interior lighting
Monitor orchard perimeter for bird activity, aphids, and cherry fruit flies

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.disease: Cercospora Leaf Spot Gray Leaf Spot
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: A devastating foliar disease of maize caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis, favored by warm temperatures and extended periods of high humidity.
symptoms: Small, tan spots with yellow halos expanding into long, narrow rectangular lesions
Lesions strictly delimited by leaf veins, measuring 1 to 5 cm in length
Lesions turn gray under humid conditions as fungal sporulation develops
Extensive blighting of entire leaves leading to stalk lodging and reduced grain fill
management: Plant corn hybrids with documented high tolerance or resistance to Gray Leaf Spot
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops like soybean or wheat for at least two seasons
Incorporate crop residue into soil to accelerate breakdown of overwintered inoculum
Apply protective foliar fungicides around tasseling (VT) stage if disease threshold is reached

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: A foliar fungal disease caused by Puccinia sorghi that attacks corn leaves, stalks, and husks under cool, humid environmental conditions.
symptoms: Small, circular to elongate reddish-brown pustules scattered across both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis, releasing powdery cinnamon-brown urediniospores
Surrounding leaf tissue turns yellow and eventually dies as pustules coalesce
Pustules turn brownish-black late in the season as teliospores develop
management: Select corn hybrids containing specific Rp gene resistance against Puccinia sorghi
Plant early in the season to avoid peak summer spore migration from southern regions
Ensure balanced soil potassium levels, which help plants resist foliar rust penetration
Scout lower leaves before tassel emergence; apply foliar fungicide if lesions appear on ear leaf

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: A destructive foliar disease caused by Exserohilum turcicum (Setosphaeria turcica), causing large cigar-shaped lesions and severe yield losses.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, grayish-green to tan lesions measuring 2.5 to 15 cm ('cigar-shaped')
Lesions not restricted by leaf veins and appear on lower leaves first, spreading upward
Dark, velvety fungal spores visible inside lesions during warm, humid mornings
Extensive blighting causing plants to look burned or frosted before maturity
management: Use corn hybrids possessing quantitative resistance and Ht resistance genes
Rotate with non-grass crops such as legumes to lower fungal spore density in field
Till infected crop debris into the soil where feasible to expedite fungal decomposition
Apply registered fungicides at early silking if lesions appear on leaves below the ear

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: The maize plant exhibits robust development with broad, dark green leaves and vigorous stalk growth.
symptoms: Foliage is broad, vibrant dark green with clean leaf blades and strong midribs
Stalks are stout, rigid, and free from internal or external discoloration
Silks and tassels emerge uniformly with complete pollination potential
Ear development shows full kernel fill without fungal ear rots
management: Follow soil test recommendations for balanced N-P-K and zinc nutrition
Maintain appropriate planting density to balance ear size and stalk strength
Provide consistent irrigation during the critical pollination and grain filling stages
Scout fields periodically for European corn borer, fall armyworm, and foliar blights

Grape___Black_rot.description: A devastating fungal disease caused by Phyllosticta ampelicida (Guignardia bidwellii) affecting all green parts of the grapevine, particularly young berries.
symptoms: Reddish-brown circular leaf spots surrounded by dark borders with tiny black dots inside
Black, elongated cankers on young shoots, petioles, and tendrils
Infected berries develop light-brown spots that quickly rot the entire fruit
Berries shrivel within days into hard, wrinkled black mummies with pimple-like fruiting bodies
management: Prune and destroy all mummified berries from the canopy and vineyard floor during dormancy
Prune grapevines to open up the canopy and promote rapid leaf drying
Apply protective fungicide sprays starting at early shoot growth through 4 weeks post-bloom
Cultivate between rows to bury fallen diseased leaf debris

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: A complex fungal trunk and foliar disease caused by a succession of wood-inhabiting fungi including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium minimum.
symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis and necrosis creating a distinctive 'tiger-stripe' leaf pattern
Small, dark circular spots ('measles') appearing on white or red grape berries
Berries crack, dry up, or drop prematurely before ripening
Wood shows internal dark streaking, vascular discoloration, and spongy white rot
management: Avoid making large pruning wounds during wet weather when fungal spores are airborne
Apply wound sealants or pruning wound paints containing protective fungicides
Remove and incinerate dead vines, infected cordons, and symptomatic wood
Disinfect pruning shears regularly with alcohol or bleach solution between vines

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: A foliar disease caused by Pseudocercospora cladosporioides (Isariopsis clavispora) causing irregular brown leaf spots and premature vine defoliation.
symptoms: Angular to irregular dark brown spots on mature leaves, often with yellow borders
Spots coalesce into large necrotic blighted areas across the leaf blade
Velvety, dark olive-brown fungal growth on the underside of older lesions
Premature leaf senescence leading to sunburned grape bunches and reduced vine reserves
management: Maintain good canopy ventilation through shoot thinning and lateral leaf removal
Apply protective copper or systemic fungicides during late spring and mid-summer
Collect and dispose of fallen diseased leaves after harvest to lower inoculum
Avoid overhead irrigation to keep foliage dry during humid periods

Grape___healthy.description: The grapevine demonstrates optimal physiological health with vibrant foliage, strong shoots, and clean bunch clusters.
symptoms: Leaves display uniform green coloration with crisp margins and clean venation
Shoots exhibit balanced vigor with healthy tendrils and active growing tips
Flower clusters and grape bunches develop cleanly without mildew or rot
Trunk and cordons show clean, intact bark without sunken lesions or galls
management: Practice balanced shoot positioning and canopy management for sunlight interception
Implement deficit irrigation management strategies to regulate berry quality
Perform periodic petiole nutrient analyses to optimize potassium and magnesium levels
Maintain a weed-free vine strip to reduce competition and insect harborages

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: A fatal bacterial disease caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri). One of the most destructive citrus diseases worldwide.
symptoms: Asymmetric, blotchy mottle chlorosis across leaf veins (unlike nutrient deficiencies)
Leaves become small, upright, thick, and leathery with raised yellow veins
Severe twig dieback and progressive canopy thinning over several seasons
Fruit is small, lopsided, remains green at the stylar end, and tastes bitter and salty
management: Aggressively monitor and control Asian citrus psyllid vectors using integrated pest management
Use certified disease-free nursery stock from screenhouse propagation facilities
Promptly scout and remove infected trees to prevent field-wide vector spread
Provide foliar micronutrient sprays (zinc, manganese, iron) to support temporary tree tolerance

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni affecting leaves, twigs, and fruit of stone fruits under warm, wet spring weather.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves turning dark purple to black
Centers of spots dry up and fall out, giving leaves a 'shot-hole' appearance
Severe leaf yellowing followed by premature defoliation from the base upward
Fruit develops pitted, sunken black spots with exudates and cracks
management: Plant peach cultivars with documented resistance to bacterial spot
Avoid planting orchards in overly sandy soils that are prone to wind-blown abrasions
Apply protective copper sprays during dormancy and early leaf emergence
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that splashes bacteria between branches

Peach___healthy.description: The peach tree displays lush, elongated green leaves with clean shoots and vigorous branch terminals.
symptoms: Leaves are deep, vibrant green, lanceolate, and free from shot-holes or curling
Terminals show active, uninterrupted vegetative shoot growth
Bark is firm and clean without gummosis, bacterial cankers, or split lesions
Developing fruit has smooth, velvety skin free from scabs or bacterial pitting
management: Prune to an open-center (vase) training system to maximize internal sun exposure
Thin developing fruit to achieve optimal fruit size and prevent limb breakage
Maintain balanced nitrogen fertilization to prevent overly rank vegetative growth
Apply dormant horticultural oils to suppress overwintering scale insects and mites

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: A common bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria attacking bell pepper foliage, stems, and fruit during warm, rainy periods.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked, circular to irregular spots on leaves turning dark brown
Spots appear slightly raised on lower leaf surface and sunken on the upper side
Severe spotting causes extensive leaf chlorosis and premature leaf drop
Fruit develops small, circular, raised, blister-like or scabby brown warts
management: Use certified disease-free, hot-water-treated seed and clean transplants
Rotate fields away from solanaceous crops (tomatoes, peppers, potatoes) for 2 to 3 years
Avoid working in or harvesting pepper fields while foliage is wet with dew or rain
Apply preventive copper-based bactericides combined with mancozeb early in the season

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: The bell pepper plant exhibits strong vegetative vigor with glossy dark-green leaves and clean floral buds.
symptoms: Foliage is dark, rich green with smooth leaf surfaces and crisp edges
Stems are sturdy and erect with healthy nodal branching
Flower buds and young fruit set evenly without blossom drop
No leaf spots, mottling, mosaic patterns, or marginal burns observed
management: Maintain uniform soil moisture using drip irrigation and plastic mulch
Ensure adequate calcium supply to prevent physiological blossom end rot
Stake or cage pepper plants to support heavy fruit loads and prevent ground contact
Inspect plants regularly for aphids, thrips, and hornworm caterpillars

Potato___Early_blight.description: A widespread fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani affecting potato and tomato foliage, stems, and tubers during alternating dry and wet periods.
symptoms: Small, dark brown to black spots developing on older lower leaves first
Lesions expand into characteristic circular patterns with concentric rings ('target board' pattern)
Yellow chlorotic halos surround advancing necrotic lesions
Severe infections cause leaves to dry up, wither, and hang down on the stem
management: Rotate crops with non-solanaceous plants such as grains or corn for at least 3 years
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation and water early in the day to allow leaves to dry
Ensure adequate nitrogen and potassium fertility; stressed plants are far more susceptible
Apply preventive fungicides (e.g., chlorothalonil or copper) when lower leaves begin to senesce

Potato___Late_blight.description: A devastating oomycete disease caused by Phytophthora infestans that can rapidly destroy entire potato fields in cool, humid, wet weather within days.
symptoms: Irregular water-soaked pale to dark green lesions on leaves turning black and purplish
White, delicate downy fungal mold visible on the underside of infected leaves in high humidity
Dark brown to black lesions rapidly expanding along petioles and main stems
Foul-smelling collapse and total rot of foliage; tubers develop dry brown granular rot
management: Plant only certified disease-free seed tubers with no signs of rot
Destroy all cull piles, volunteer potato plants, and infected tubers before planting season
Select late blight-resistant potato cultivars whenever available in your region
Apply protective fungicides before rain events when weather forecasts indicate cool, wet conditions

Potato___healthy.description: The potato plant displays vigorous, healthy canopy development with deep green compound leaves and sturdy stems.
symptoms: Compound leaves are deep green, robust, and free from target-spots or blights
Stems are upright, sturdy, and free of dark streaks or water-soaked cankers
Underground stolons develop uniform tubers free from internal discoloration
Foliage shows balanced vegetative growth without excessive spindliness
management: Hill soil properly around potato stems to protect developing tubers from light and pests
Provide consistent soil moisture, avoiding waterlogging or excessive drying cycles
Apply balanced fertilizers according to soil test recommendations
Monitor plants weekly for Colorado potato beetles, leafhoppers, and early blight signs

Raspberry___healthy.description: The raspberry plant exhibits clean cane development, vibrant trifoliate foliage, and healthy flowering shoots.
symptoms: Leaves are rich green with clean serrated margins and silvery undersides
Primocanes and floricanes are sturdy without purple spots, spurs, or lesions
Lateral fruiting shoots are vigorous with strong floral trusses
No spur blight, anthracnose lesions, or cane botrytis observed
management: Prune out spent floricanes immediately after fruit harvest to reduce fungal spore pressure
Trellis canes effectively to allow maximum air movement and sunlight penetration
Mulch root zones to maintain cool root temperatures and suppress weed competition
Maintain good soil drainage; raspberries are highly sensitive to standing water

Soybean___healthy.description: The soybean crop displays healthy trifoliate leaves with uniform green color and vigorous nodal growth.
symptoms: Trifoliate leaves are clean, broad, vibrant green with no pustules or mosaic mottling
Stems show strong branching with firm nodes and healthy trifoliate emergence
Active nitrogen-fixing root nodules exhibit pink or red interior cross-sections
Pod set is uniform across main stem nodes without premature pod abortion
management: Inoculate soybean seed with Bradyrhizobium japonicum before planting in new fields
Practice crop rotation with corn or small grains to break soil-borne disease cycles
Ensure proper planting depth and soil temperature (above 15°C) for rapid germination
Scout canopy for soybean aphids, bean leaf beetles, and sudden death syndrome

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: A very common fungal disease caused by Podosphaera xanthii (Erysiphe cichoracearum) attacking cucurbit leaves, petioles, and stems in warm, dry weather.
symptoms: Talcum-like white powdery fungal spots appearing on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Spots rapidly enlarge to cover entire leaf blades, petioles, and young stems
Infected leaves turn yellow, become brittle and brown, and die prematurely
Loss of foliage leads to sunscalded fruit, poor fruit flavor, and reduced harvest duration
management: Choose powdery mildew-resistant or tolerant squash varieties
Space plants generously to promote good air circulation through the cucurbit canopy
Apply protective bio-fungicides, neem oil, or potassium bicarbonate at the very first white speck
Remove and compost or dispose of heavily infected older leaves at the base of vines

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: A fungal disease caused by Diplocarpon earlianum that affects strawberry foliage, petioles, runners, and calyxes.
symptoms: Small, irregular purple to dark brownish spots developing on the upper leaf surface
Spots coalesce causing the leaf blade tissue between spots to turn reddish-purple then brown
Leaf margins curl upward and appear scorched or burned by fire
Severe defoliation weakens strawberry crowns and reduces subsequent season yields
management: Plant certified disease-free strawberry runner plants in well-drained raised beds
Mow and remove older foliage immediately after the renovation of June-bearing beds
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip tape beneath plastic mulch to keep foliage dry
Apply protective fungicides early in spring as new leaf growth commences if disease history exists

Strawberry___healthy.description: The strawberry plant shows healthy trifoliate leaves with deep green color and vigorous crown development.
symptoms: Trifoliate leaves are glossy, deep emerald green with clean, sharply serrated margins
Crowns are firm, sturdy, and free from red stele root rot or anthracnose cankers
Flower trusses and developing green fruit show clean sepals and white petals
Runners are healthy and establish vigorous daughter plants with clean roots
management: Plant in well-drained raised beds with rich organic matter and a soil pH of 6.0 to 6.8
Use straw or black plastic mulch to keep fruit and leaves from touching bare soil
Maintain consistent soil moisture with drip irrigation throughout flowering and fruiting
Scout for two-spotted spider mites, thrips, and slugs on fruit and leaf undersides

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: A destructive bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas vesicatoria species affecting tomato foliage, stems, and fruit under warm, rainy, and windy conditions.
symptoms: Small (2-3 mm), dark brown, water-soaked circular to angular leaf spots
Spots may have a greasy appearance and are surrounded by a faint yellow halo
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow, dry out, and drop prematurely, causing sunscald on fruit
Fruit develops small, raised, black, scabby blister-like spots with sunken centers
management: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants from reputable commercial suppliers
Rotate out of solanaceous crops (tomatoes, peppers, potatoes) for at least 3 seasons
Disinfect stakes, cages, tools, and greenhouse equipment between crops
Apply preventive copper bactericide combined with mancozeb before rainy periods

Tomato___Early_blight.description: A very common fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani affecting leaves, stems, and fruit. Favored by warm temperatures and heavy dew or frequent rain.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with distinct concentric rings ('target board' appearance)
Lesions appear on oldest lower leaves first and progress upward through the canopy
Leaf tissue around lesions turns yellow, followed by leaf blighting and collapse
Dark, sunken, leathery cankers develop on stems and fruit near the calyx end
management: Prune lower leaves (bottom 30 cm) to prevent soil-splash onto foliage during rains
Mulch around tomato stems with clean straw or plastic to create a soil barrier
Stake or trellis plants to maintain upright growth and promote airflow
Apply protective organic bio-fungicides or chlorothalonil at the earliest signs of spotting

Tomato___Late_blight.description: A catastrophic oomycete disease caused by Phytophthora infestans that can destroy entire tomato plantings within a few days under cool, humid weather.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked, greasy gray-green lesions on leaves turning dark brown
White, fuzzy fungal sporulation visible on the underside of infected leaves in moist air
Dark brown, greasy lesions expanding rapidly along petioles and main stems
Fruit develops firm, dark brown, wrinkled, leathery rot with greasy texture
management: Avoid planting tomatoes near potatoes that could harbor overwintered blight
Inspect plants twice weekly during cool (15-22°C), persistently wet or foggy weather
Destroy and bag heavily infected plants immediately; do not compost late blight debris
Apply preventive fungicides before predicted cool wet spells in blight-prone areas

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: A fungal disease caused by Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum), common in greenhouses and high tunnels with relative humidity exceeding 85%.
symptoms: Pale green to pale yellow chlorotic spots with indefinite margins on upper leaf surfaces
Dense, olive-green to grayish-brown velvety mold growth on the corresponding lower surface
Infected leaves wither, curl, turn brown, and drop prematurely from the bottom up
Fruit is rarely infected, but defoliation significantly reduces fruit size and yield
management: Maximize ventilation and airflow in greenhouses and high tunnels using exhaust fans
Keep greenhouse relative humidity below 85% by heating and venting simultaneously
Choose tomato varieties with high genetic resistance to Passalora fulva races
Use drip irrigation and avoid wetting tomato foliage during watering

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: One of the most destructive foliar diseases of tomato caused by Septoria lycopersici. Usually appears after fruit set and spreads rapidly in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Numerous small (2-3 mm) circular spots with dark brown margins and light gray or white centers
Tiny black speck-like fruiting bodies (pycnidia) clearly visible in the center of spots
Leaves turn yellow around spots, curl up, become brown, and drop off
Defoliation begins at the base of the plant and rapidly progresses upward, exposing fruit to sunscald
management: Cleanly remove and discard infected lower leaves as soon as first spots appear
Apply organic mulch (straw, woodchips) around the base of plants to stop spore splash from soil
Never overhead-water; use soaker hoses or drip irrigation exclusively
Apply protective copper or organic fungicide sprays on a 7 to 10 day schedule in wet weather

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: A destructive pest infestation caused by Tetranychus urticae that feeds on plant cell contents, heavily favored by hot, dry, dusty environmental conditions.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (tiny dots) on the upper surface of leaves
Leaves become bronzed, pale, and dry, eventually taking on a papery burned look
Delicate, fine silk webbing visible on the undersides of leaves and between stems
Tiny red or yellow-orange eight-legged mites visible moving under leaf magnification
management: Wash leaf undersides with strong streams of water to dislodge mites and reduce dust
Introduce natural predatory mites such as Phytoseiulus persimilis in greenhouse environments
Apply insecticidal soap, neem oil, or horticultural mineral oil covering leaf undersides thoroughly
Maintain adequate plant watering; drought-stressed tomatoes are far more vulnerable

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: A fungal disease caused by Corynespora cassiicola attacking tomato foliage, stems, and fruit under warm, humid conditions with frequent rains.
symptoms: Small, pinpoint water-soaked spots on leaves enlarging into brown lesions with concentric rings
Lesions are circular to irregular with light brown centers and dark brown margins
Premature leaf yellowing and defoliation, exposing fruit to sunburn
Fruit develops small, circular, slightly sunken brown lesions that crack as fruit ripens
management: Prune plants to improve airflow and facilitate rapid drying of the inner canopy
Rotate fields away from solanaceous crops, cucurbits, and cotton for at least two seasons
Avoid overhead irrigation and maintain adequate plant row spacing
Apply preventive fungicide sprays (e.g., copper, azoxystrobin, or chlorothalonil)

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A serious viral disease caused by a Begomovirus (TYLCV), transmitted exclusively by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Causes severe plant stunting and floral abortion.
symptoms: Leaves are markedly reduced in size, curl strongly upward, and become cup-shaped
Prominent yellowing (chlorosis) along leaf margins and between veins
Severe stunting of the entire tomato plant with shortened internodes giving a bushy look
Flowers drop prematurely before setting fruit; fruit set is drastically reduced
management: Plant tomato varieties possessing genetic resistance to TYLCV (e.g., Ty-1, Ty-3 genes)
Manage whitefly populations using yellow sticky traps, insect exclusion screens, and insecticidal soaps
Remove and bag infected plants immediately to prevent whiteflies from spreading the virus
Control weed hosts (nightshades, mallow) around field margins that harbor the virus

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A highly stable, contagious viral disease (ToMV) closely related to Tobacco Mosaic Virus, transmitted easily by mechanical contact, contaminated tools, seeds, and workers' hands.
symptoms: Alternating light green and dark green mosaic or mottled patches on leaves
Leaves become puckered, distorted, and in severe cases thin into a 'shoestring' or 'fern-leaf' shape
Plant growth is stunted, especially when infected at an early seedling stage
Fruit may show internal brown necrotic rings ('brownwall') and uneven ripening
management: Plant certified virus-free seed and ToMV-resistant tomato varieties
Wash hands with soap and water and disinfect tools with a 20% nonfat dry milk or bleach solution
Avoid smoking or handling tobacco products before touching tomato plants
Carefully pull and dispose of infected plants to prevent mechanical transmission to neighbors

Tomato___healthy.description: The tomato plant exhibits optimal physiological health with vigorous foliage, robust stems, and clean flower trusses.
symptoms: Foliage is vibrant, deep emerald green with clean, unblemished leaflets
Main stems and branches are thick, sturdy, and covered with healthy trichomes (hairs)
Blossom clusters develop evenly with healthy yellow flowers and successful fruit set
No spotting, curling, mosaic patterns, or premature leaf senescence observed
management: Provide consistent drip irrigation to maintain uniform soil moisture and prevent cracking
Apply balanced tomato fertilizer with adequate calcium to prevent blossom end rot
Stake, cage, or trellis plants to maintain clean upright growth off the ground
Prune redundant suckers selectively to optimize fruit size and canopy airflow
